clue.text: Butterfly gives a firm penetrating nip

indicators.note: the words for a firm go right through the bite, sitting inside it

parts.note: a nip is a small bite, a peck
CO is the usual abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: Someone describes a business delivering a sharp bite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butterfly' looks like a swimming stroke or a flutter of nerves, but it names the insect species.
explanation.definitionFit: The peacock is a common European butterfly with eyespots on its wings.

clue.text: Somewhere to display ornaments before barrier goes up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up reads the word from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: ere is an old word for before
a gate is a barrier

explanation.surface: A display case is put out before a barrier rises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes up' reverses both pieces together, making ETAGERE.
explanation.definitionFit: An étagère is a set of open shelves for showing off ornaments and bric-a-brac.

clue.text: In Paris, it's protecting royal crown

indicators.note: the French phrase protects the letter by surrounding it

parts.note: c'est is French for it is
R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN

explanation.surface: A French note that some royal crown is being guarded.
explanation.definitionFit: A crest is the top of something, such as a hill or a head, its crown.

clue.text: College bird defending Victor's 25

indicators.note: the bird surrounds the letter as if defending it

parts.note: a heron is a wading bird
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A college bird shields Victor's medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 25 refers to the answer at 25, BADGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A chevron is a V-shaped stripe on a uniform sleeve showing rank, a type of badge.

clue.text: Shepherd spoils Prince Harry

parts.note: to mar something is to spoil it, so 'spoils' is mars
Prince Hal is Shakespeare's name for the young Henry V, called Harry

explanation.surface: A tabloid line: a guide ruins things for the royal prince.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince Harry' looks modern, but this is Shakespeare's Prince Hal from Henry IV.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to guide or herd people into order, as an official marshals a crowd.

clue.text: Utter a bombastic speech about Republican

indicators.note: the speech words go about the party letter, placed around it

parts.note: a rant is a loud, bombastic speech

explanation.surface: A politician delivers a tirade about a Republican.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utter' is not the verb to speak but the adjective meaning complete.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrant means complete or out-and-out, as in arrant nonsense.

clue.text: Stay to drink beer left in first-class

parts.note: to sup is to drink
porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: An invitation to remain and have a beer in first class.
explanation.walkthrough: A second route also works: PORT (left, on a ship) inside SUPER (first-class).
explanation.definitionFit: A stay is a prop or brace, something giving support.

clue.text: A 19 goes up each day in old chopper

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up reads the word backwards

parts.note: the answer at 19 is a witch; a hex is a witch, from German Hexe

explanation.surface: A witch rises each day carrying an ancient blade.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 is SORCERESS, here meaning HEX, a witch; 'goes up' turns HEX into XEH.
explanation.definitionFit: An axehead is the blade of an axe, a tool for chopping.

clue.text: Some call for rocks round, say, place to get one's bearings

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the abbreviation
to rock is to shake about, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: eg (for example) is a common way of saying 'say'

explanation.surface: A caller asks for rocks to help find their way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bearings' are heraldic devices on a coat of arms, not directions.
explanation.definitionFit: The College of Arms in London grants coats of arms, whose heraldic devices are called bearings.

clue.text: Familiar eastern soft drink lacking colour

parts.note: a familiar is a close friend, a pal

explanation.surface: An everyday Asian soft drink that has no colour to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue offers two routes: PAL + E (familiar, eastern), and P + ALE (soft, drink), P being piano, the musical mark for soft.
explanation.definitionFit: Something washed out and without much colour is described as wan or faded.

clue.text: European earned rent, having boosted self-image

parts.note: to get money is to earn it, so 'earned' is got
rent, past tense of rend, means torn, ripped

explanation.surface: A European landlord's rental income has made them vain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' is not money paid for a flat but the past tense of rend, to tear.
explanation.definitionFit: An ego trip is an act done to flatter one's vanity, so someone on one has inflated their own image.

clue.text: Inventor of Morse put off by cuts

indicators.note: the multiplication sign cuts into the verb, breaking it open

parts.note: to put someone off is to deter them
'by' means times in multiplication, written as the sign X

explanation.surface: Someone asks who devised Morse code and was then discouraged by spending cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: Not Samuel Morse of the code: Colin Dexter wrote the Inspector Morse detective novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Colin Dexter created the Oxford detective Inspector Morse, famous from the British TV series.

clue.text: City dweller, recluse entertains prof

indicators.note: a host entertains a guest by holding them inside, so the recluse word holds the academic

parts.note: a recluse keeps to themselves, a loner
a don is a university teacher, like a professor

explanation.surface: A town resident who keeps to themselves has an academic over for dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident of London, the City, is a native of the capital.

clue.text: Somebody English ousts American in cleric's place

indicators.note: one letter ousts another, taking its place in the house word

parts.note: a parsonage is the house provided for a parson

explanation.surface: A tale of an Englishman taking over a vicarage from an American.
explanation.definitionFit: A personage is a person of importance, a somebody rather than a nobody.

clue.text: Tours curse small area beside Belle Vue regularly

parts.note: an acre is a measure of area

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter

explanation.surface: Tourists swear at a small plot beside the old Manchester pleasure ground of Belle Vue.
explanation.walkthrough: Tours is the French city, so this is a French oath.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacrebleu is a dated French exclamation of surprise or anger, an oath.

clue.text: Film companies getting rid of ten hunks

indicators.note: dropping letters from the film word, so they are removed

parts.note: film companies are studios
IO looks like the number 10 written with letters

explanation.surface: Movie firms are laying off ten handsome leading men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting rid of' removes IO (10 written as letters) from STUDIOS.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud is slang for a sexually attractive man, as a hunk is.

clue.text: Double starts to take wonder drug

indicators.note: the starts of the next two words are their first letters

parts.note: ice is slang for crystal methamphetamine

explanation.surface: Someone takes a second dose of a miracle medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something twice is to do it doubly, two times over.

clue.text: Guardian staff apparently love new style Arsenal

parts.note: newspaper staff write of themselves as we in editorials
AP is the shortened form of apparently, its first letters
love is nil in tennis, the letter O
NS stands for New Style, dates in the Gregorian calendar

explanation.surface: Journalists at the Guardian are said to adore the football club's fresh way of playing.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal is not the London football club but a store of arms. New Style dating replaced the Old Style Julian calendar in Britain in 1752.
explanation.definitionFit: An arsenal is a stock of arms and armaments, a nation's collected guns and bombs.

clue.text: Witch or goddess on board

indicators.note: to be on board is to be inside the ship, so the following letters go within it

parts.note: board here stands for a ship, SS being steamship
Ceres is the Roman goddess of agriculture

explanation.surface: A question of whether a woman aboard ship is a witch or a deity.
explanation.walkthrough: SS, for steamship, is the crossword's usual ship, so anything 'on board' goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorceress is a female magician, a woman using spells.

clue.text: 26 has one county singer sent up

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending up reads the word backwards

parts.note: a tenor is a singer

explanation.surface: A singer from a county is mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is NOBLEWOMAN; 'sent up' turns TENOR into RONET.
explanation.definitionFit: A peeress wears a small crown at ceremonies such as coronations, showing her rank.

clue.text: Large duke suddenly starts confining guards

indicators.note: the verb confines the two letters inside it

parts.note: a horse shies when it starts suddenly in fright

explanation.surface: A big duke jumps in fright and has guards hold him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suddenly starts' is a jump in fright, SHIES, which wraps L and D.
explanation.definitionFit: To shield someone is to protect or guard them.

clue.text: Fine cow could be Daisy

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils
a cow is something that lows, moos

explanation.surface: A cow named Daisy is a fine one.
explanation.walkthrough: Daisy is a common name for a cow, but here it is the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The daisy is a common example of a bloom.

clue.text: Desert ship, having trouble withdrawing plant

parts.note: the camel is called the ship of the desert

indicators.note: withdrawing makes the word draw back, read in reverse

parts.note: to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: A camel's trouble withdrawing from a plant it has been eating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'withdrawing' turns AIL into LIA.
explanation.definitionFit: The camellia is a flowering evergreen shrub related to the tea bush.

clue.text: Novice player's rare and rather absorbing book

indicators.note: the phrase for rather soaks up the book letter inside it

parts.note: a bit means rather, as in rather tired

explanation.surface: A beginner's book that is rare and rather engrossing.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a rabbit is a poor or novice player, especially at golf or tennis, or a weak batsman in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporting slang names a weak or inexperienced player after the timid animal.

clue.text: Mark's invited around midnight

indicators.note: the past tense goes around the letter

parts.note: bade, past tense of bid, means invited
the middle of the word night is its G

explanation.surface: Mark is invited out around twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: A badge is a mark or token of identity, rank or membership.

clue.text: Lady's about to retire wasted old staff

indicators.note: to retire is to draw back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: on means about, as in a talk on art
to blow money is to waste it, so 'wasted' is blew
to staff a post is to man it

explanation.surface: A woman is about to retire after squandering her old workforce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to retire' turns ON into NO.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lady in British titles is a peeress or other titled woman of rank.

clue.text: As expected, judge left for Germany at start of month

indicators.note: one letter is left behind for another, a swap
the swap happens at the first letter of the month

parts.note: July is a month
D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)

explanation.surface: A judge departs for Germany at the start of a month, as planned.
explanation.definitionFit: Duly means properly and at the expected time, as things ought to happen.

clue.text: Groom queries polite title

indicators.note: to groom is to tidy and rearrange, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A bridegroom asks questions about a courteous form of address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' looks like the definition, a bridegroom or a squire, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Esq. is a courtesy suffix added to a man's name in formal letters.

clue.text: He can't believe that he is taking part in this

definitions.text: He can't believe that he is taking part in this

indicators.note: the word sits as part of the phrase in this clue, inside its letters

explanation.surface: Someone sceptical says he does not believe in what he is doing.
explanation.walkthrough: The word lies within 'thAT HE IS Taking', and the whole clue describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: An unbeliever who denies that any god exists cannot believe in religion.
